title: The tree with roots above
hookLine: chapter fifteen opens with a sacred fig tree growing upside down
carry: the world is a tree rooted in God

lines: THE OLD PEEPAL IN THE VILLAGE.
cards: A huge old peepal tree stands at the edge of a village square. Threads are tied around its trunk. Someone walks slow circles around it.
Two old men sit in its shade and argue about cricket. Its heart-shaped leaves tremble in the slightest breeze. It's the sacred fig, the ashvattha.
Now flip that tree over in your mind: roots up in the sky, branches hanging down, spreading all over the earth. That strange picture is how chapter fifteen begins.

teach.b: Verse one. They speak of an undying ashvattha tree with its roots above and its branches below.

Its leaves are the Vedic hymns. Whoever knows this tree knows the Vedas. Back in chapter ten, Krishna said that among trees he is the ashvattha, and many Hindus point to that line when they honor the peepal.
So what's the tree? Commentators read it as the whole world of change, samsara, the round of birth and death. Its roots are above because it grows from the highest source.
Verse two: its branches spread up and down, fed by the three gunas, and its buds are the objects of the senses. Some roots stretch downward too, into the human world, tangling us in action.

That's why the tree feels so real: we're hanging in its branches, and the branches keep growing. Verse three is honest: its real shape can't be seen from here, not its end, not its beginning, not what it stands on.
Then the surprise. This huge, deep-rooted tree, Krishna says, cut it down with the strong axe of non-attachment.

Asanga, not clinging. Not with violence, not by running away, but by letting go. Verse four: then seek that place from which no one returns, and take refuge in the first person, from whom this ancient flow came.
Verse six says that place isn't lit by sun, moon or fire.
This stretch ran through the field, humility, the one light, the three threads, how they show up, and going beyond them. Today it all becomes one picture.

how: The peepal (ashvattha, sacred fig) is honored by Hindus: some water it, tie threads around it and walk around it; Gita 15 uses it as an image of the world, and some recite chapter fifteen on its own.

o: the banyan, whose roots drop down from its branches
the sacred fig, the peepal, rooted above in Gita 15
the lotus, a flower rising clean out of the mud

games.q: the upside-down tree — tap the pairs.
p: a home no sun, moon or fire lights

s: the upside-down tree appears only in the Gita
the Katha Upanishad also describes an eternal fig with roots above.
the Gita says to cut the tree with the axe of non-attachment
the tree's buds are the objects of the senses
verse 2: fed by the gunas, budding with sense objects.

games.q: you're tangled in a huge tree whose roots you can't even see. what does Krishna tell you to do?
o: cut it with the strong axe of non-attachment.
study it until you know every branch.
games.why: cut it with non-attachment. verse 3 admits its shape can't be seen from here; the way out is letting go.

practice: Picture yourself among the branches of a great tree, each branch something you hold on to: a plan, a worry, a person, a wish.

Feel your grip on one, and without dropping anything, loosen it a little; that's the axe the Gita means, not clinging. Then let your attention travel up the trunk toward the roots, the source, and rest there.

wordCard.voice: Ashvattha, the sacred fig. Gita fifteen: the world of change as an upside-down tree, rooted in the highest, cut with the axe of not clinging.

orig.note: Sanskrit: ashvattha, the sacred fig (peepal), Ficus religiosa; the upside-down tree of Gita 15.1.

carryVoice: Your line: the world is a tree rooted in God. Roots in the highest, branches in our lives. Day two hundred ten, complete.
